original_title: Gabe Newell on Steam monopoly accusations: Gamers have 'enormous choice' about where to buy games
summary_en: Valve chief Gabe Newell has pushed back against accusations of Steam holding a monopoly on PC gaming. During a court testimony, Newell asserted that players possess abundant options for purchasing games across various platforms.
ai_analysis: Gabe Newell's defense of Steam's market position highlights the ongoing tension between platform dominance and consumer choice in the PC gaming landscape.

en.title: Gabe Newell Says Gamers Have 'Enormous Choice' Amid Steam Monopoly Claims
en.summary: Valve chief Gabe Newell has pushed back against accusations of Steam holding a monopoly on PC gaming. During a court testimony, Newell asserted that players possess abundant options for purchasing games across various platforms.
en.body:
In a recent court testimony, **Gabe Newell**, co-founder of Valve, directly addressed the persistent accusations that **Steam** wields a monopolistic grip on PC game distribution. Responding to a lawsuit filed by **Wolfire Games** in 2021, Newell asserted that gamers today have "enormous choice" regarding where they purchase their digital entertainment.

Newell elaborated on this point, stating that consumers can opt to buy games not only on **Steam** but also on platforms like **Xbox**, the **Epic Games Store**, or even directly from software developers. This perspective directly challenges the core complaint of the lawsuit, which alleges that Valve actively suppresses competition by preventing developers from offering lower prices on competing storefronts. **Wolfire Games** founder **David Rosen** previously claimed that Valve threatened to remove his game, **Overgrowth**, from **Steam** if he dared to sell it at a reduced price elsewhere, even on his own website without **Steam** keys or DRM.

> "Customers have enormous choice" about where they purchase their games, Newell testified, including "whether they buy the game on an Xbox, whether they buy it on Steam, whether they buy it on Epic Games Store or whether they buy it directly from software developers."

During his testimony, **Newell** repeatedly denied the existence of any such "unwritten rule" or policy that dictates pricing on other platforms. He even stated that he was confused when asked about Valve's potential reaction to such a scenario, suggesting that "many of our partners and many of our customers are quite happy with the service that we're providing." This defense, however, stands in stark contrast to the experiences shared by some developers and the sentiment expressed in online communities where a significant portion of developers reportedly believe **Steam** does indeed hold a monopoly, with some noting that Valve "is definitely putting their thumb heavily on the scale of controlling who are winners and losers in PC gaming."

## The Developer Dilemma

The debate over **Steam**'s market power is not merely an academic exercise; it has tangible implications for game developers striving to reach audiences and remain profitable. While **Steam** offers unparalleled reach and a robust feature set for players, its dominance can create a challenging environment for smaller studios or those seeking flexible pricing strategies. The lawsuit and **Newell**'s testimony highlight the complex interplay between platform economics, developer autonomy, and consumer access in the ever-evolving landscape of digital game sales.

## Looking Ahead

As this legal battle continues, the industry will be closely watching for any rulings or further statements that could shape the future of PC game distribution. The outcome may influence how platforms operate and how developers are able to set prices for their games across the multitude of storefronts available today. Details on future court proceedings have not yet been announced.

Steam, oyunculara erişimi ve oyunları satın almaları için birçok seçeneği sunuyor, ancak bu dominance, küçük stüdyolar veya fiyatlandırma stratejileri konusunda esneklik isteyen geliştiriciler için zor bir ortam yaratıyor. es.title: Gabe Newell Desmiente Acusaciones de Monopolio de Steam
es.summary: El fundador de Valve, Gabe Newell, ha desmentido en un testimonio en la corte las acusaciones de que Steam tiene un monopolio en la distribución de juegos para PC. Según Newell, los jugadores tienen una amplia variedad de opciones para comprar juegos en diferentes plataformas.
es.body:
En un reciente testimonio en la corte, **Gabe Newell**, co-fundador de Valve, abordó directamente las persistentes acusaciones de que **Steam** tiene un control monopolístico sobre la distribución de juegos para PC. Respondiendo a una demanda presentada por **Wolfire Games** en 2021, Newell afirmó que los jugadores de hoy en día tienen una "amplia elección" sobre dónde comprar sus entretenimiento digital.

Newell explicó este punto, afirmando que los consumidores pueden optar por comprar juegos no solo en **Steam**, sino también en plataformas como **Xbox**, la **Tienda de Juegos de Epic Games** o incluso directamente de los desarrolladores de software. Esta perspectiva desafía directamente la queja central de la demanda, que alega que Valve suprime activamente la competencia impidiendo a los desarrolladores ofrecer precios más bajos en tiendas competidoras. El fundador de **Wolfire Games**, **David Rosen**, había afirmado previamente que Valve amenazó con eliminar su juego, **Overgrowth**, de **Steam** si él se atrevía a venderlo a un precio reducido en otra plataforma, incluso en su propio sitio web sin claves de Steam o DRM.

> "Los clientes tienen una amplia elección sobre dónde comprar sus juegos", testificó Newell, incluyendo "si compran el juego en un Xbox, si lo compran en Steam, si lo compran en la Tienda de Juegos de Epic Games o si lo compran directamente de los desarrolladores de software".

Durante su testimonio, **Newell** negó repetidamente la existencia de cualquier "regla no escrita" o política que dictamine los precios en otras plataformas. Incluso afirmó que estaba confundido cuando se le preguntó sobre la posible reacción de Valve en tal escenario, sugiriendo que "muchos de nuestros socios y muchos de nuestros clientes están muy contentos con el servicio que estamos proporcionando". Esta defensa, sin embargo, se opone a las experiencias compartidas por algunos desarrolladores y el sentimiento expresado en las comunidades en línea donde una gran parte de los desarrolladores cree que **Steam** en realidad tiene un monopolio, con algunos destacando que Valve "definitivamente está poniendo su dedo en el timón de controlar quiénes son los ganadores y perdedores en el juego de PC".

## El Dilema del Desarrollador

La discusión sobre el poder de mercado de **Steam** no es meramente un ejercicio académico; tiene implicaciones tangibles para los desarrolladores de juegos que buscan llegar a audiencias y mantenerse rentables. Si bien **Steam** ofrece una alcance sin precedentes y un conjunto de características robusto para los jugadores, su dominio puede crear un entorno desafiante para los estudios más pequeños o aquellos que buscan estrategias de precios flexibles. La demanda y el testimonio de **Newell** resaltan la interacción compleja entre la economía de las plataformas, la autonomía del desarrollador y el acceso del consumidor en la constante evolución del mercado de ventas de juegos digitales.

## Próximos Pasos

A medida que esta batalla legal continúa, la industria estará atenta a cualquier decisión o declaración que pueda moldear el futuro de la distribución de juegos para PC. El resultado puede influir en cómo operan las plataformas y cómo los desarrolladores pueden establecer precios para sus juegos en las múltiples tiendas disponibles en la actualidad. Los detalles sobre futuros procedimientos judiciales no han sido anunciados.

content_raw: Back in 2023, a court ordered Valve chief Gabe Newell to testify, in person , in the long-running antitrust suit filed by Wolfire Games in 2021. A new report by Bloomberg runs down some of what Newell had to say during that testimony, including a denial that Steam holds any kind of monopoly on PC gaming. Or is even an overly dominant force. "Customers have enormous choice" about where they purchase their games, Newell testified, including "whether they buy the game on an Xbox, whether they buy it on Steam, whether they buy it on Epic Games Store or whether they buy it directly from software developers." Newell also denied the existence of an alleged 'unwritten rule' that prevents developers from offering their games at lower prices on non-Steam storefronts. That's one of the central complaints behind Wolfire's lawsuit: Founder David Rosen said in 2021 that when he asked Valve about offering his studio's game Overgrowth at a reduced price on other stores,"they replied that they would remove Overgrowth from Steam if I allowed it to be sold at a lower price anywhere, even from my own website without Steam keys and without Steam's DRM." Asked about this rule, Newell repeatedly denied it exists, even when shown internal communications seemingly showing Valve employees enforcing it: "Valve does not have a policy or practice of dictating prices to third-party software developers on other platforms." When asked how Valve would react if it ever happened, Newell initially said he was confused by the question and then added, "Many of our partners and many of our customers are quite happy with the service that we're providing." That's certainly true, as far as it goes. Games aren't getting any cheaper and there's a good likelihood that Grand Theft Auto 6 will usher in the era of the $80 videogame , but Steam sales remain massively popular because holy cow, there's a ton of good stuff and you can get it dirt cheap . Steam has also helped break the grip that major publishers had over conventional retail sales, opening the door to real fame and fortune for lucky indie devs. At the same time, Steam is, if not a monopoly, awfully close to one: It is so deeply entrenched that Epic Games has spent years literally giving away its games, and has barely made a dent—in fact, New Blood boss Dave Oshry said earlier this year that Epic freebies were great for sales on Steam . The Epic launcher is admittedly not an optimal experience , but a big challenge Epic Games faces is simply that an awful lot of gamers don't seem to want an effective Steam competitor: Steam rules the roost, and they like it that way. A big majority of game developers, meanwhile, reckons that Steam really does hold a monopoly on the PC games market.
